title: Meeting Benny Goodman at Eddie Tancil's; the tea dance
summary: At sixteen he hears the young Goodman sit in, is thrilled and invites him to the Columbus Park tea dances.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Well tell me something now. That's a fascinating thing that you've just said. But you worked with Benny Goodman and everybody knows he's certainly very, very famous.
Oh yes.
And Glen Miller who was indeed
famous when he went down in his airplane during the war.
That's right.
Suppose you tell me a little bit about them as they were, as you knew them. As, yes.
Well, surely. Benny Goodman, well he, I finally met Benny Goodman at a place called Eddie (Tansils?).
Eddie what?
Eddie Tansils.
TANCIL?

Yes, that's right. It was a nightclub and they had a bar. And it was just at the dividing line of Cicero Avenue and Hawthorne. And Cicero is where Capone moved in there. And Capone, it was right next to a race track, the Hawthorne Race Track out in the West Side of Chicago. Near the Western Electric industry there.

And I was playing with a guy by the name of (Frisco Hassy?) and his Quartett in this band and Benny Goodman, the trombone player, Joey (Cantrelle?) was talking about this kid Benny Goodman on clarinet, he was you know, so terrific. And I said, well man, where is he, bring him up. And Benny Goodman came up and at this

time I was sixteen years old. I just started, playing professionally from the Austin Highschool Gang. But I was very apt and I went ahead. And so he brought Benny Goodman out one night and this kid is in short pants. (LAUGHTER). And I'm just in long pants. I just got in long pants.
At sixteen, yes.
And I want you to know at that time....
You came out of knickers?
That's true.
Right, I know.

And I want you to know I was wearing bell bottoms and I had a bush haircut just like I have now. (LAUGHTER). That's how long ago that was. It's fifty years ago. So Benny Goodman came out and that son of a gun sat in and started playing that clarinet and I'm telling you. He played a tune by the name of 'Rose of the Rio Grande'. And man I just flipped at this kid for playing the clarinet the way he did. And he was marvellous.
So I told him I said look, we've got a band out there at Austin High you know, come on out and join us. And at that time I started to run a tea dance, tea (dance ?) the dancers
we used to call them you know, real high class style.
Yes.

Tea dance at the Columbus Park Refectory . And charge a quarter admission and I believe it was Saturday afternoons, yes. And we used to play for them for the money and then I'd pay the guys you know. I'd pay them a little. Not too much. And because I was the leader then. And I invited Benny out and he played for nothing and he, you know nothing. Because we already had a clarinet player.
It's been a long time since he's played for nothing. (LAUGHTER).
Well he was just a kid.
I understand he's worse, he's worse than, as bad as Bob Hope almost. (LAUGHTER).

He's rather frugal, I don't blame him. However, he used to come out and play with us there and he joined the Austin High Gang for a while. But then when he got to go with Benny Pollack. I've forgotten my premise here. I go off in a tangent.
